def: A ligand is an ion or molecule that donates a pair of electrons to a central metal atom/ion to form a coordinate bond. Coordination number is the total number of such donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal.
points: Ligands have at least one lone pair of electrons to donate (Lewis base), metal is Lewis acid.
Unidentate ligands donate through one atom, e.g. Cl-, NH3, H2O.
Bidentate ligands donate through two atoms, e.g. ethylenediamine (en), oxalate (ox).
Polydentate ligands donate through many atoms, e.g. EDTA (hexadentate).
Ambidentate ligands can bond through either of two different atoms, e.g. SCN- (via S or N).
Coordination number = number of sigma bonds between ligands and central metal, e.g. [Co(NH3)6]3+ has CN = 6.
Common coordination numbers are 4 (tetrahedral/square planar) and 6 (octahedral).
formula: CN = number of donor atoms bonded to central metal

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Ligand type"] --> B["Unidentate - one donor atom"]
  A --> C["Bidentate - two donor atoms"]
  A --> D["Polydentate - many donor atoms"]
  A --> E["Ambidentate - two possible donor atoms"]

example: [Ni(CO)4]: Ni is central metal, CO is unidentate ligand, coordination number = 4 (tetrahedral geometry).
tip: State the definition, give one example of each ligand type, and clearly write the coordination number with geometry for full marks.

def: IUPAC nomenclature of coordination compounds follows fixed rules to name the ligands first (in alphabetical order), then the central metal with its oxidation state in Roman numerals.
points: Name ligands in alphabetical order before the metal name, regardless of charge.
Anionic ligands end in 'o' (chloro, cyano, oxalato); neutral ligands keep usual name (ammine for NH3, aqua for H2O, carbonyl for CO).
Use prefixes di, tri, tetra for simple ligands; bis, tris for complex/bidentate ligand names.
If the complex ion is an anion, the metal name ends in '-ate'.
Oxidation state of the metal is written in Roman numerals in brackets right after the metal name.
Cation is named before anion in the full compound name, just like simple salts.
formula: Name = (ligands alphabetically) + (metal) + (oxidation state in Roman numerals)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Write ligands alphabetically"] --> B["Add prefix for number of ligands"]
  B --> C["Write metal name"]
  C --> D["Add -ate if complex is anion"]
  D --> E["Write oxidation state in brackets"]

tip: Practice naming 5-6 standard complexes both ways (formula to name and name to formula) - this is asked almost every year.

def: Isomerism in coordination compounds occurs when two or more compounds have the same formula but different arrangement of ligands, leading to different properties.
points: Structural isomerism arises from different bonding patterns: ionisation, linkage, coordination, and hydrate isomerism.
Ionisation isomers give different ions in solution, e.g. [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 and [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br.
Linkage isomerism occurs with ambidentate ligands like SCN-, which can bind through S or N.
Stereoisomerism includes geometrical isomerism (cis-trans) in square planar and octahedral complexes.
Optical isomerism occurs when a complex and its mirror image are non-superimposable (chiral), common in octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands.
Geometrical isomers differ in physical/chemical properties even though bonds are the same, only arrangement differs.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Isomerism"] --> B["Structural - ionisation, linkage, coordination"]
  A --> C["Stereoisomerism"]
  C --> D["Geometrical - cis and trans"]
  C --> E["Optical - mirror images"]

example: [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] square planar complex has cis form (two Cl adjacent) and trans form (two Cl opposite) as geometrical isomers.
tip: Draw the cis and trans structures clearly with labels - diagram-based questions on this topic carry good marks.

def: Valence Bond Theory explains the bonding, geometry and magnetic nature of coordination compounds using hybridisation of the metal's orbitals to accept ligand electron pairs.
points: Central metal ion uses hybrid orbitals (sp3, dsp2, sp3d2, d2sp3) to accept lone pairs from ligands.
If inner (n-1)d orbitals are used for hybridisation, complex is called inner orbital/low spin complex.
If outer nd orbitals are used, complex is called outer orbital/high spin complex.
Strong field (low spin) complexes pair up electrons, often making them diamagnetic.
Weak field (high spin) complexes keep electrons unpaired, making them paramagnetic.
Geometry is decided by the type of hybridisation: sp3 gives tetrahedral, dsp2 gives square planar, sp3d2/d2sp3 give octahedral.
formula: Hybridisation types: sp3 (tetrahedral), dsp2 (square planar), sp3d2 or d2sp3 (octahedral)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Metal ion orbitals"] --> B["Hybridise with ligand lone pairs"]
  B --> C["Inner d orbitals used - low spin"]
  B --> D["Outer d orbitals used - high spin"]
  C --> E["Often diamagnetic"]
  D --> F["Often paramagnetic"]

example: [Ni(CN)4]2-: Ni2+ uses dsp2 hybridisation, square planar, diamagnetic (all electrons paired due to strong CN- field).
tip: Always connect hybridisation to geometry AND magnetic behaviour in your answer - examiners look for all three.

def: Crystal Field Theory explains bonding in coordination compounds as a purely electrostatic interaction between the central metal ion and the ligands, which splits the d-orbitals into different energy levels.
points: In an octahedral field, the five degenerate d orbitals split into two sets: lower energy t2g (3 orbitals) and higher energy eg (2 orbitals).
The energy gap between t2g and eg is called crystal field splitting energy, denoted delta-o.
Strong field ligands (like CN-, CO) cause large splitting, giving low spin complexes.
Weak field ligands (like F-, H2O) cause small splitting, giving high spin complexes.
In tetrahedral complexes, splitting pattern is reversed and smaller: e set lower, t2 set higher.
Electrons fill according to Hund's rule balanced against the crystal field splitting energy (pairing energy vs delta-o).
formula: Octahedral splitting: delta-o separates t2g (lower) and eg (higher) orbitals

diagram.draw: Draw two horizontal energy levels. Draw a dashed horizontal line below both labelled 'average energy of d orbitals'. Draw the lower level with 3 small boxes labelled t2g below the dashed line. Draw the upper level with 2 small boxes labelled eg above the dashed line. Mark the vertical gap between them with an arrow labelled delta-o.

example: [CoF6]3-: F- is weak field ligand, small delta-o, electrons spread out (high spin), 4 unpaired electrons, paramagnetic.
tip: Draw the t2g-eg splitting diagram neatly with delta-o marked - this diagram alone often fetches 1-2 marks.

def: Coordination compounds are used widely in analytical chemistry, extraction of metals, biological systems and medicine because of their unique bonding and selective reactivity.
points: Used in qualitative/quantitative analysis, e.g. Ni2+ detected as red precipitate with DMG (dimethylglyoxime).
EDTA (a hexadentate ligand) is used to estimate hardness of water and to treat heavy metal poisoning.
Used in extraction of metals, e.g. silver and gold are extracted as cyanide complexes [Ag(CN)2]-.
Biological systems use coordination compounds: haemoglobin (iron complex) carries oxygen, chlorophyll (magnesium complex) helps photosynthesis.
Coordination compounds like cisplatin [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] (cis isomer) are used as anti-cancer drugs.
Electroplating uses complex ions to get smooth, uniform metal deposits.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Coordination compounds"] --> B["Analysis - Ni-DMG test"]
  A --> C["Metal extraction - Ag and Au cyanide complex"]
  A --> D["Biology - haemoglobin, chlorophyll"]
  A --> E["Medicine - cisplatin anti-cancer drug"]

example: Hardness of water is estimated by titrating Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions against EDTA solution using an indicator.
tip: List at least 4 different application areas with one specific example each - breadth of answer earns more marks than depth on one point.
